questions.q: Which structural and functional features distinguish electrical synapses from chemical synapses in the human nervous system?
options: Electrical synapses use connexon gap-junction channels for direct bidirectional ionic current flow with virtually zero synaptic delay (~0.1 ms), whereas chemical synapses use neurotransmitter exocytosis across a 20-40 nm cleft with a ~0.5-1.0 ms synaptic delay
Electrical synapses rely on calcium-dependent SNARE vesicle fusion across a 50 nm cleft
Chemical synapses allow direct cytoplasmic continuity and faster transmission than electrical synapses
Electrical synapses are unidirectional whereas chemical synapses are always bidirectional
questions.explain: Electrical synapses couple adjacent neurons via hexameric connexon hemichannels (gap junctions) for ultra-fast synchronous firing (e.g., brainstem respiratory/oculomotor nuclei, retina, cardiac/smooth muscle), while chemical synapses provide signal amplification, sign inversion (inhibition), and synaptic plasticity.

open.q: Contrast electrical and chemical synapses across three structural or functional properties (cleft width, transmission mechanism, synaptic delay, or directionality).
accept: Electrical synapses have ~3.5 nm gap junctions (connexons), direct bidirectional ion flow, and virtually no delay (~0.1 ms); chemical synapses have a 20-40 nm cleft, neurotransmitter exocytosis, unidirectional transmission, and ~0.5-1 ms delay
Gap-junction bidirectional direct current without delay vs vesicular unidirectional neurotransmitter release with synaptic delay

questions.q: Which ion influx into the presynaptic axon terminal directly triggers synaptic vesicle docking, priming, and exocytotic fusion with the active zone membrane?
options: Sodium (Na+) influx through fast Nav channels
Calcium (Ca2+) influx through voltage-gated P/Q-type and N-type Ca2+ channels
Potassium (K+) efflux through delayed rectifier channels
Chloride (Cl-) influx through GABA-A receptors
questions.explain: Arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic bouton opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Cav2.1/Cav2.2); Ca2+ enters down its steep electrochemical gradient and binds synaptotagmin to trigger vesicle fusion.

open.q: Which ion enters the presynaptic terminal upon arrival of an action potential to trigger neurotransmitter exocytosis?
accept: Calcium
Ca2+
Calcium ions

questions.q: Which vesicular protein acts as the primary fast Ca2+ sensor that triggers SNARE-mediated synaptic vesicle fusion upon Ca2+ entry into the presynaptic terminal?
options: Synapsin I
Clathrin
Synaptotagmin
Acetylcholinesterase
questions.explain: Ca2+ binding to the C2 domains of vesicular synaptotagmin displaces complexin and drives the SNARE complex (vesicular synaptobrevin/VAMP + target-membrane syntaxin and SNAP-25) to zipper together and fuse the membranes.

open.q: Name the vesicular Ca2+-sensing protein and the three core SNARE proteins required for synaptic vesicle exocytosis.
accept: Synaptotagmin (Ca2+ sensor); synaptobrevin (VAMP), syntaxin, and SNAP-25 (SNAREs)
Synaptotagmin; VAMP/synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25

questions.q: How do botulinum neurotoxin (Clostridium botulinum) and tetanus neurotoxin (Clostridium tetani) produce flaccid versus spastic paralysis despite both being zinc-dependent endoproteases that cleave SNARE proteins?
options: Botulinum toxin destroys muscle actin; tetanus toxin blocks renal sodium channels
Both toxins act exclusively on the cerebral motor cortex
Botulinum toxin increases acetylcholine synthesis; tetanus toxin blocks dopamine reuptake
Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release at the NMJ; tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory GABA/glycine release in the CNS
questions.explain: Both cleave SNAREs (synaptobrevin, SNAP-25, or syntaxin), but differential axonal transport targets peripheral cholinergic motor terminals (botulism) versus spinal inhibitory interneurons (tetanus disinhibition).

open.q: Explain why cleavage of SNARE proteins by botulinum toxin causes flaccid paralysis whereas cleavage by tetanus toxin causes spastic paralysis.
accept: Botulinum toxin blocks peripheral acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction (flaccid paralysis), while tetanus toxin undergoes retrograde transport to spinal inhibitory interneurons and blocks glycine/GABA release (spastic paralysis)
Peripheral blockade of excitatory ACh release vs central blockade of inhibitory glycine/GABA release

questions.q: How is acetylcholine (ACh) synthesized inside cholinergic nerve terminals and packaged into synaptic vesicles?
options: Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) combines choline and acetyl-CoA in the cytosol, and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) loads ACh into vesicles via H+ antiport
Acetylcholinesterase synthesizes ACh inside the synaptic cleft
Tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine to ACh inside mitochondria
Glutamate decarboxylase converts glutamate to ACh inside the Golgi apparatus
questions.explain: Rate-limiting high-affinity Na+-dependent choline uptake (CHT1) imports choline, ChAT synthesizes ACh in the cytoplasm, and VAChT concentrates ACh into vesicles (inhibited by vesamicol; choline uptake is blocked by hemicholinium).

open.q: Name the enzyme that synthesizes acetylcholine from choline and acetyl-CoA, and identify the rate-limiting step in acetylcholine synthesis.
accept: Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT); high-affinity Na+-dependent choline uptake into the nerve terminal
ChAT; choline reuptake

questions.q: What type of receptor is the adult skeletal muscle motor end-plate nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (Nm), and what ionic conductance change occurs when two molecules of ACh bind to it?
options: Gi-protein-coupled metabotropic receptor that opens K+ channels
Pentameric ligand-gated non-selective cation channel (alpha2-beta-epsilon-delta) that opens to admit Na+ and extrude K+, producing a depolarizing end-plate potential (EPP)
Tyrosine kinase receptor that phosphorylates actin directly
Ligand-gated Cl- channel that hyperpolarizes the sarcolemma
questions.explain: Simultaneous binding of two ACh molecules to the two alpha subunits opens the central cation pore; because Na+ has a much larger inward driving force than outward K+ at -90 mV, net Na+ influx depolarizes the end-plate toward ~0 mV (reversal potential).

open.q: Describe the ion movements and reversal potential (~0 mV) when acetylcholine opens nicotinic receptors at the skeletal muscle motor end-plate.
accept: Simultaneous Na+ influx and K+ efflux through a non-selective cation channel, with greater inward Na+ current producing depolarization toward ~0 mV
Net Na+ entry exceeding K+ exit through a ligand-gated cation channel

questions.q: Why does a single motor nerve action potential at a healthy mammalian neuromuscular junction virtually always trigger a skeletal muscle action potential (high safety factor)?
options: Because the motor end-plate potential (EPP) is an all-or-none spike
Because acetylcholine never degrades in the synaptic cleft

Because a single nerve impulse releases ~100-200 quanta of ACh, generating a large graded EPP (~50-70 mV depolarization) that far exceeds the ~30-40 mV depolarization needed to reach threshold of adjacent Nav1.4 channels in junctional folds
Because gap junctions directly connect motor axons to muscle fibers
questions.explain: Each quantum (~5,000-10,000 ACh molecules) produces a miniature end-plate potential (MEPP ~0.4-0.5 mV); synchronous release of >100 quanta produces an EPP of ~50-70 mV, providing a 3- to 5-fold safety factor above threshold.

open.q: What is a miniature end-plate potential (MEPP), and how does it relate to the full end-plate potential (EPP)?
accept: MEPP (~0.4-0.5 mV) is the small depolarization caused by spontaneous exocytosis of a single ACh vesicle (quantum); an EPP is the summation of ~100-200 simultaneous MEPPs triggered by a nerve action potential
Spontaneous single-vesicle quantum depolarization; full EPP is the sum of many quanta

questions.q: How is acetylcholine action terminated in the neuromuscular junction synaptic cleft?
options: Intact acetylcholine is transported directly back into the nerve terminal
Monoamine oxidase (MAO) oxidizes acetylcholine in mitochondria
Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) methylates acetylcholine
Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) anchored in the basal lamina rapidly hydrolyzes ACh into choline and acetate, followed by Na+-dependent reuptake of choline
questions.explain: AChE is one of the fastest known enzymes (~25,000 ACh molecules hydrolyzed per second per active site), clearing ACh within <1 ms so the end-plate can repolarize and respond to the next impulse.

open.q: Name the enzyme that terminates acetylcholine signaling at the neuromuscular junction and state its two hydrolysis products.
accept: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE); choline and acetate
AChE breaks ACh down into choline and acetic acid (acetate)

questions.q: How do competitive non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (such as tubocurarine or rocuronium) differ in mechanism from depolarizing blockers (such as succinylcholine)?
options: Non-depolarizing drugs competitively block Nm receptors; succinylcholine persistently activates them and causes depolarisation block
Non-depolarizing drugs inhibit acetylcholinesterase; succinylcholine blocks presynaptic calcium channels
Succinylcholine is rapidly destroyed by synaptic acetylcholinesterase
Both drug classes act only on receptors in the central nervous system
questions.explain: Curare/rocuronium compete with ACh at the alpha subunit (overcome by raising cleft ACh with neostigmine), whereas succinylcholine resists AChE (hydrolyzed slowly by plasma butyrylcholinesterase), holding the end-plate depolarized so surrounding Nav1.4 channels stay inactivated.

open.q: Contrast the mechanism of neuromuscular blockade by rocuronium (non-depolarizing) versus succinylcholine (depolarizing).
accept: Rocuronium competitively blocks nicotinic ACh receptors without activating them; succinylcholine persistently activates and depolarizes the end-plate, inactivating adjacent voltage-gated Na+ channels
Competitive receptor antagonism vs sustained end-plate depolarization causing Na+ channel inactivation

questions.q: Which ionic permeability changes typically generate an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) versus a fast inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP)?
options: EPSP: opening of Cl- or K+ channels; IPSP: opening of Na+ channels

EPSP: opening of ligand-gated non-selective cation (Na+/K+) channels shifting Vm toward ~0 mV; IPSP: opening of ligand-gated Cl- channels (GABA-A/glycine) or G-protein-coupled K+ channels (GABA-B/M2) shifting Vm toward ECl (~-75 mV) or EK (~-90 mV)
EPSP: closure of all membrane channels; IPSP: opening of L-type Ca2+ channels
Both EPSP and IPSP are caused by identical Na+ influx
questions.explain: Any conductance whose reversal potential is above firing threshold (~-55 mV) is excitatory (EPSP), whereas any conductance whose reversal potential is below threshold (ECl, EK) is inhibitory (IPSP)—even if ECl equals resting potential ('shunting inhibition').

open.q: Explain what 'shunting inhibition' is when GABA-A Cl- channels open in a neuron whose resting membrane potential (-70 mV) already equals ECl (-70 mV).
accept: Opening Cl- channels increases membrane conductance (lowers membrane resistance Rm), short-circuiting incoming excitatory currents and reducing the amplitude of concurrent EPSPs even without hyperpolarizing the cell
Increased Cl- conductance drops Rm (Ohm's law V = I*R) and clamps Vm near ECl, attenuating depolarizing EPSPs

questions.q: How do temporal summation and spatial summation differ during postsynaptic integration of graded potentials?
options: Temporal summation occurs across different neurons; spatial summation occurs over time at one synapse
Temporal summation applies only to inhibitory potentials; spatial summation only to excitatory potentials
Temporal summation combines successive inputs at one synapse; spatial summation combines inputs from multiple synapses
Neither form of summation can influence firing at the axon hillock
questions.explain: A single CNS EPSP (~0.5-1 mV) is usually far below the ~15 mV depolarization needed to reach threshold at the axon hillock, requiring combined temporal and spatial summation to trigger a spike.

open.q: Distinguish temporal summation from spatial summation at postsynaptic neurons, and name the cable constant governing each.
accept: Temporal summation adds successive inputs at a single synapse over time (time constant tau); spatial summation adds simultaneous inputs from multiple synapses across space (length constant lambda)
Repeated firing at one synapse (tau) vs simultaneous firing at multiple synapses (lambda)

questions.q: Why do inhibitory synapses on a multipolar neuron cluster disproportionately on the soma and axon initial segment (axosomatic and axoaxonic synapses) rather than on distal dendritic tips?
options: Distal dendrites lack phospholipid bilayers
Strategic placement near the spike trigger zone (axon hillock) maximizes their ability to shunt and veto summated excitatory currents arriving from the entire dendritic tree
GABA receptors cannot function in dendritic membranes
Axosomatic synapses amplify EPSPs tenfold
questions.explain: Because passive currents decay exponentially with distance (lambda), placing inhibitory shunting conductance right at the soma/initial segment gives inhibition maximal leverage over action potential initiation.

open.q: Why are inhibitory synapses typically concentrated on the neuronal soma and axon initial segment rather than on distal dendrites?
accept: Positioning near the axon hillock maximizes shunting and control over whether summated dendritic EPSPs reach firing threshold
Strategic proximity to the spike trigger zone gives inhibitory inputs maximum leverage to prevent action potential initiation

questions.q: What is the mechanism of presynaptic inhibition at an axoaxonic synapse in the central nervous system (such as on primary sensory Ia afferents in the spinal cord)?
options: Hyperpolarisation of the postsynaptic motor neuron by glycine
Destruction of postsynaptic glutamate receptors by proteases
GABA at an axoaxonic synapse reduces presynaptic calcium entry and transmitter release
Direct electrical coupling between the inhibitory axon and postsynaptic dendrite
questions.explain: Presynaptic inhibition selectively dampens transmitter output from a specific afferent pathway (improving sensory contrast/lateral inhibition) while leaving the postsynaptic neuron fully responsive to other excitatory inputs.

open.q: Explain the mechanism and functional advantage of presynaptic inhibition compared to postsynaptic inhibition.
accept: An axoaxonic synapse (typically GABAergic) reduces presynaptic action potential amplitude and Ca2+ entry, decreasing neurotransmitter release from that specific terminal without hyperpolarizing or altering responsiveness of the postsynaptic neuron to other inputs
Reduces Ca2+ influx and transmitter release at a single afferent terminal selectively

questions.q: How does presynaptic facilitation (for example, serotonin-mediated sensitization in Aplysia or cAMP-PKA signaling in CNS terminals) increase neurotransmitter release?
options: By opening voltage-gated Cl- channels in the presynaptic terminal
By activating Gs-cAMP-PKA to phosphorylate and close presynaptic K+ channels, prolonging action potential duration so voltage-gated Ca2+ channels stay open longer and admit more Ca2+
By inhibiting synaptotagmin
By accelerating acetylcholinesterase activity
questions.explain: Broadening the presynaptic action potential increases integrated Ca2+ entry during depolarization, boosting vesicle fusion probability.

open.q: Describe how closure of presynaptic K+ channels produces presynaptic facilitation.
accept: Closing K+ channels slows repolarization and prolongs the presynaptic action potential, keeping voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open longer to increase Ca2+ influx and neurotransmitter release
Prolonged presynaptic spike duration increases Ca2+ entry and vesicle exocytosis

questions.q: Which amino acid is the primary fast excitatory neurotransmitter throughout the brain and spinal cord?
options: Glutamate
Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)
Glycine
Serotonin (5-HT)
questions.explain: Glutamate mediates the vast majority of fast excitatory neurotransmission in the CNS via ionotropic AMPA, kainate, and NMDA receptors as well as metabotropic mGluRs.

open.q: Name the primary fast excitatory neurotransmitter in the human central nervous system and its three ionotropic receptor subtypes.
accept: Glutamate; AMPA, NMDA, and kainate receptors
L-glutamate; AMPA, kainate, and NMDA

questions.q: Which two amino acid neurotransmitters serve as the primary fast inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain and in the spinal cord/brainstem, respectively?
options: Glutamate in the brain; aspartate in the spinal cord
GABA in the brain; glycine (alongside GABA) in the spinal cord and brainstem
Dopamine in the brain; histamine in the spinal cord
Acetylcholine in the brain; norepinephrine in the spinal cord
questions.explain: GABA (synthesized from glutamate by glutamic acid decarboxylase using vitamin B6/pyridoxal phosphate) is the major brain inhibitory transmitter, while glycine (antagonized by strychnine) is the major inhibitory transmitter of spinal Renshaw cells and Ia inhibitory interneurons.

open.q: Name the enzyme and vitamin cofactor required to synthesize GABA from glutamate, and name the spinal cord poison that blocks glycine receptors.
accept: Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) and vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate); strychnine
GAD with pyridoxal phosphate (B6); strychnine

questions.q: Why does the ionotropic NMDA glutamate receptor function as a molecular 'coincidence detector' essential for Hebbian synaptic plasticity?
options: Because it opens only when GABA and glycine bind simultaneously
Because it conducts only chloride ions during sleep

Because opening its Ca2+/Na+-permeable pore requires BOTH presynaptic glutamate binding (plus co-agonist glycine/D-serine) AND postsynaptic depolarization to expel the extracellular Mg2+ ion blocking its pore
Because it is permanently open at -90 mV without any ligand
questions.explain: At resting membrane potential (-70 mV), extracellular Mg2+ plugs the NMDA channel pore; strong postsynaptic depolarization (via AMPA receptors) electrostatically expels Mg2+, allowing Ca2+ influx to activate CaMKII and trigger long-term potentiation (LTP).

open.q: State the two simultaneous requirements needed for Ca2+ to flow through an NMDA glutamate receptor channel.
accept: Presynaptic glutamate (and glycine/D-serine co-agonist) binding PLUS postsynaptic depolarization to expel the Mg2+ pore block
Ligand binding (glutamate + co-agonist) and postsynaptic depolarization to remove Mg2+ blockade

questions.q: How do benzodiazepines (such as diazepam) and barbiturates (such as phenobarbital) differ in their allosteric modulation of the GABA-A chloride channel?
options: Benzodiazepines block GABA-A channels; barbiturates activate NMDA channels

Benzodiazepines increase the FREQUENCY of GABA-A channel opening (requiring endogenous GABA), whereas barbiturates increase the DURATION of channel opening and at high doses can directly open the pore without GABA
Barbiturates increase opening frequency; benzodiazepines directly open the channel in the absence of GABA
Both drugs act exclusively on metabotropic GABA-B receptors
questions.explain: Because benzodiazepines only potentiate endogenous GABA (increasing opening frequency), they have a ceiling effect and wider therapeutic index than barbiturates, which prolong open duration and directly gate Cl- channels at overdose levels (causing fatal respiratory depression).

open.q: Contrast how benzodiazepines and barbiturates alter GABA-A receptor chloride channel gating kinetics.
accept: Benzodiazepines increase frequency of channel opening (GABA-dependent); barbiturates increase duration of channel opening (and directly open channels at high doses)
Frequency of opening (benzodiazepines) vs duration of opening (barbiturates)

questions.q: Which step is the rate-limiting enzymatic reaction in the synthesis of catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine)?
options: Conversion of L-tyrosine to L-DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase (using tetrahydrobiopterin, O2, and Fe2+)
Conversion of L-DOPA to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase
Conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine by dopamine beta-hydroxylase
Conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine by PNMT
questions.explain: Tyrosine hydroxylase is regulated by end-product feedback inhibition and phosphorylation (inhibited clinically by metyrosine); PNMT (phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase) requires high local cortisol in the adrenal medulla to methylate norepinephrine to epinephrine.

open.q: Write the sequential biosynthetic pathway from tyrosine to epinephrine, naming each enzyme in order.
accept: Tyrosine -> (tyrosine hydroxylase) -> L-DOPA -> (DOPA decarboxylase) -> Dopamine -> (dopamine beta-hydroxylase) -> Norepinephrine -> (PNMT) -> Epinephrine
Tyrosine hydroxylase, aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, PNMT

questions.q: Which brainstem nuclei are the principal sources of central noradrenergic, serotonergic, and histaminergic projections across the brain?
options: Substantia nigra (norepinephrine), red nucleus (serotonin), and cerebellum (histamine)
Locus coeruleus in the pons (norepinephrine), medullary/pontine raphe nuclei (serotonin/5-HT), and tuberomammillary nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus (histamine)
Basal nucleus of Meynert (dopamine), amygdala (glycine), and thalamus (epinephrine)
Subthalamic nucleus (serotonin), globus pallidus (histamine), and hippocampus (norepinephrine)
questions.explain: Diffuse ascending modulatory arousal systems originate in discrete nuclei: locus coeruleus (NE), raphe nuclei (5-HT, synthesized from tryptophan), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine, from histidine), basal forebrain/pedunculopontine nuclei (ACh), and VTA/substantia nigra (dopamine).

open.q: Identify the primary brainstem or hypothalamic source nucleus for: (1) norepinephrine, (2) serotonin, and (3) histamine in the CNS.
accept: 1) Locus coeruleus, 2) Raphe nuclei, 3) Tuberomammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus
Locus coeruleus (NE), raphe nuclei (5-HT), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine)

questions.q: How is the synaptic action of monoamine neurotransmitters (norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin) primarily terminated?
options: Extracellular enzymatic cleavage in the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase
High-affinity Na+/Cl--dependent presynaptic reuptake transporters (NET, DAT, SERT), followed by vesicular repackaging via VMAT or intracellular degradation by MAO and COMT
Diffusion into cerebrospinal fluid without any reuptake
Binding to postsynaptic myosin heads
questions.explain: Unlike ACh (which is degraded in the cleft), catecholamines and 5-HT are cleared mainly by presynaptic plasma membrane transporters (the targets of SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, and cocaine).

open.q: State the primary mechanism terminating the action of catecholamines and serotonin in the synaptic cleft and name the two main intracellular/tissue degradative enzymes.
accept: Presynaptic reuptake via Na+-dependent transporters (NET, DAT, SERT); degraded by monoamine oxidase (MAO) and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT)
Presynaptic transporter reuptake; MAO and COMT

questions.q: How do neuropeptides (such as substance P, endorphins, enkephalins, NPY, and CGRP) differ from classical small-molecule neurotransmitters in their synthesis, storage, and release?
options: Neuropeptides are synthesized in the axon terminal by cytosolic enzymes and cleared by rapid presynaptic reuptake

Neuropeptides are synthesized as prepropeptides on rough ER in the neuronal soma, packaged in the Golgi into large dense-core vesicles transported via fast axonal transport, require higher-frequency Ca2+ bursts for release, and are terminated by extracellular peptidases without reuptake
Neuropeptides bind exclusively to fast ligand-gated Na+ channels
Neuropeptides are never co-released with small-molecule neurotransmitters
questions.explain: Co-transmission (coexistence of a fast small-molecule transmitter in small clear vesicles and a slow modulatory neuropeptide in large dense-core vesicles) allows a single neuron to produce different effects depending on firing frequency.

open.q: List three differences between neuropeptides and small-molecule neurotransmitters regarding synthesis site, vesicle type, or clearance mechanism.
accept: Neuropeptides are synthesized in the soma (ribosomes/ER/Golgi) rather than axon terminal, stored in large dense-core vesicles rather than small clear vesicles, and cleared by extracellular peptidases/diffusion without presynaptic reuptake
Soma synthesis + axonal transport, large dense-core vesicles, and lack of reuptake

questions.q: How do endocannabinoids (anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol) and nitric oxide (NO) act as 'retrograde messengers' at central synapses?
options: They are stored in presynaptic vesicles and released before an action potential arrives

They are synthesized on demand in the postsynaptic neuron upon depolarization/Ca2+ rise and diffuse backward across the synaptic cleft to modulate presynaptic neurotransmitter release (via presynaptic CB1 Gi receptors or soluble guanylyl cyclase)
They permanently destroy the presynaptic axon terminal
They travel from the spinal cord to the cerebral cortex in blood vessels
questions.explain: Retrograde messengers violate classical one-way signaling: postsynaptic Ca2+ elevation triggers synthesis of lipophilic endocannabinoids or gaseous NO, which diffuse retrogradely to inhibit presynaptic Ca2+ channels (depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition/excitation) or enhance release.

open.q: What is a retrograde synaptic messenger, and name two examples in the central nervous system.
accept: A messenger synthesized in the postsynaptic cell on demand that diffuses backward to modulate the presynaptic terminal; endocannabinoids (anandamide/2-AG) and nitric oxide (NO)
Postsynaptic-to-presynaptic diffusible signal; endocannabinoids and nitric oxide

questions.q: What cellular mechanism underlies long-term potentiation (LTP) in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons following high-frequency tetanic stimulation?
options: Removal of all AMPA receptors from the postsynaptic density

Postsynaptic depolarization expels Mg2+ from NMDA receptors, allowing Ca2+ influx that activates CaMKII, driving insertion of additional AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane and enhancing dendritic spine growth
Permanent blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
Conversion of glutamate into glycine
questions.explain: Early LTP involves CaMKII phosphorylation and exocytotic insertion of GluA1-containing AMPA receptors into silent synapses, while late LTP requires CREB-mediated gene transcription and new protein synthesis for structural spine remodeling.

open.q: Summarize the postsynaptic receptor changes that mediate hippocampal CA1 long-term potentiation (LTP).
accept: NMDA receptor Ca2+ influx activates CaMKII, leading to phosphorylation and insertion of additional AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane (plus CREB-dependent protein synthesis in late LTP)
Activation of NMDA receptors triggers CaMKII-mediated trafficking of new AMPA receptors to the synapse

questions.sub: Synaptic Properties: Delay, Fatigue, Convergence, Divergence
questions.q: How do 'convergence' and 'divergence' in neuronal circuits support spinal and cortical processing?
options: Convergence allows multiple presynaptic inputs to summate onto a single postsynaptic neuron (integration), whereas divergence allows a single neuron to branch and excite/inhibit thousands of downstream target neurons (amplification)
Convergence occurs only in sensory receptors; divergence occurs only in smooth muscle
Both terms refer to synaptic fatigue during prolonged stimulation
Divergence reduces the number of active neurons to one
questions.explain: An alpha motor neuron receives thousands of converging excitatory and inhibitory inputs from cortex, brainstem, and spinal interneurons, while a single corticospinal or sensory neuron diverges to coordinate entire muscle synergies.

open.q: Contrast neuronal convergence and divergence in central nervous system circuits.
accept: Convergence: multiple presynaptic neurons synapse onto a single postsynaptic neuron (integration); Divergence: one presynaptic neuron branches to synapse onto many postsynaptic targets (amplification)
Many-to-one integration (convergence) vs one-to-many amplification (divergence)

questions.sub: Synaptic Properties: Delay, Fatigue, Convergence, Divergence
questions.q: What is 'synaptic fatigue' during prolonged, repetitive high-frequency stimulation of an excitatory synapse, and what is its protective physiological role?
options: Complete depletion of postsynaptic actin filaments
Repeated activity exhausts the readily releasable vesicle pool faster than it can be replenished
Permanent death of the presynaptic neuronal cell body
Overproduction of myelin around the postsynaptic membrane
questions.explain: When firing frequency outpaces vesicle recycling and transmitter synthesis, EPSP amplitude declines progressively, preventing sustained epileptiform discharges.

open.q: Explain the mechanism of synaptic fatigue and its protective function in the central nervous system.
accept: Depletion of readily releasable presynaptic neurotransmitter vesicles faster than synthesis/recycling; protects against excessive neuronal overexcitation and seizures
Exhaustion of presynaptic transmitter stores that dampens runaway CNS excitation

questions.sub: Synaptic Properties: Delay, Fatigue, Convergence, Divergence
questions.q: What is 'post-tetanic potentiation' (PTP) following a brief train of high-frequency presynaptic stimuli?
options: A transient enhancement of postsynaptic potential amplitude lasting seconds to a few minutes, caused by residual Ca2+ accumulation in the presynaptic terminal increasing vesicle release probability
Permanent loss of synaptic transmission
Hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane to -120 mV
Destruction of all synaptic cleft enzymes
questions.explain: During a brief tetanus, Ca2+ enters faster than presynaptic mitochondria and Ca2+ pumps can clear it; residual Ca2+ binds high-affinity release sensors so subsequent single impulses release more quanta.

open.q: What causes post-tetanic potentiation (PTP) immediately after a brief high-frequency burst of presynaptic action potentials?
accept: Residual calcium accumulation inside the presynaptic terminal increases the probability of synaptic vesicle exocytosis for subsequent impulses
Elevated residual presynaptic Ca2+ boosting neurotransmitter release

questions.q: How does Renshaw cell recurrent inhibition regulate alpha motor neuron firing in the spinal cord?
options: Alpha motor neuron axon collaterals release glutamate onto Renshaw cells

Alpha motor neuron recurrent axon collaterals release acetylcholine to excite Renshaw interneurons, which in turn release glycine (and GABA) to inhibit the same and synergistic alpha motor neurons, stabilizing motor output and preventing excessive discharge
Renshaw cells excite gamma motor neurons to cause muscle spasm
Renshaw cells inhibit sensory dorsal root ganglion cells only
questions.explain: Renshaw cells provide negative-feedback recurrent inhibition (and inhibit Ia inhibitory interneurons—recurrent facilitation), fine-tuning motor firing rates; tetanus toxin blocks Renshaw glycine release.

open.q: Name the excitatory neurotransmitter released by alpha motor neuron collaterals onto Renshaw cells and the inhibitory neurotransmitter released by Renshaw cells back onto alpha motor neurons.
accept: Acetylcholine (onto Renshaw cells) and glycine (onto alpha motor neurons)
ACh and glycine

questions.q: What is 'reciprocal innervation' (reciprocal inhibition) in spinal motor control?
options: Simultaneous maximal contraction of both agonist and antagonist muscles across a joint
Excitation of an agonist alpha motor neuron pool accompanied by simultaneous disynaptic inhibition (via Ia inhibitory interneurons releasing glycine) of the antagonist muscle's alpha motor neurons
Inhibition of both agonist and antagonist muscles during walking
Direct electrical coupling between flexor and extensor motor neurons
questions.explain: When Ia afferents from biceps muscle spindles excite biceps alpha motor neurons, collateral branches excite Ia inhibitory interneurons that hyperpolarize triceps alpha motor neurons, allowing smooth joint movement.

open.q: Explain the synaptic circuit mediating reciprocal inhibition during a stretch or voluntary movement.
accept: Group Ia afferents (or descending motor tracts) excite agonist alpha motor neurons while simultaneously exciting glycinergic Ia inhibitory interneurons that inhibit antagonist alpha motor neurons
Excitation of agonist motor neurons paired with interneuron-mediated inhibition of antagonist motor neurons

questions.sub: Synaptic Properties: Delay, Fatigue, Convergence, Divergence
questions.q: How do 'reverberating (oscillatory) neuronal circuits' function in the central nervous system?
options: Positive-feedback collateral branches re-excite earlier neurons in the chain, generating sustained rhythmic output (as in brainstem respiratory rhythmogenesis and wakefulness) until synaptic fatigue or external inhibition terminates the loop
They completely block all sensory input to the thalamus
They convert action potentials into hormones
They occur only in peripheral tendons
questions.explain: Reverberating circuits prolong brief trigger signals into sustained rhythmic discharges, such as inspiratory ramp generation in the pre-Botzinger complex.

open.q: Describe the structural organization of a reverberating neuronal circuit and give one physiological example of its function.
accept: Axon collaterals feed back onto earlier neurons in the pathway to sustain repetitive firing; example: brainstem respiratory rhythm generation or short-term working memory
Positive feedback loop of collateral synapses sustaining rhythmic output, such as breathing rhythm

questions.q: How do ionotropic GABA-A receptors and metabotropic GABA-B receptors differ in their signaling mechanisms and speed of inhibition?
options: GABA-A is a fast pentameric ligand-gated Cl- channel (fast IPSP), whereas GABA-B is a slow Gi/o-protein-coupled receptor that opens GIRK K+ channels postsynaptically and inhibits voltage-gated Ca2+ channels presynaptically (slow IPSP)
GABA-A is coupled to Gs proteins; GABA-B is a ligand-gated Na+ channel
Both GABA-A and GABA-B open voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
GABA-B is blocked by bicuculline; GABA-A is activated by baclofen
questions.explain: GABA-A (targeted by benzodiazepines, barbiturates, propofol, and alcohol) mediates rapid millisecond Cl- inhibition, while GABA-B (activated by the muscle relaxant baclofen) mediates slower, longer-lasting K+-mediated hyperpolarization and presynaptic Ca2+ inhibition.

open.q: Contrast GABA-A and GABA-B receptors in terms of receptor class, effector ion channels, and clinical pharmacology.
accept: GABA-A: ionotropic Cl- channel (modulated by benzodiazepines/barbiturates); GABA-B: metabotropic Gi/o GPCR that opens K+ channels and closes Ca2+ channels (activated by baclofen)
Fast ligand-gated Cl- channel vs slow G-protein-coupled K+/Ca2+ channel modulator

questions.q: How do D1-like (D1, D5) and D2-like (D2, D3, D4) dopamine receptors differ in their intracellular G-protein coupling?
options: D1-like receptors couple to Gs (increasing cAMP), whereas D2-like receptors couple to Gi/o (decreasing cAMP, opening K+ channels, and closing Ca2+ channels)
D1-like receptors couple to Gi; D2-like receptors couple to Gs
Both D1 and D2 receptors are ligand-gated Na+ channels
Neither D1 nor D2 receptors are expressed in the basal ganglia
questions.explain: In the basal ganglia striatum, excitatory D1 receptors facilitate the direct movement pathway while inhibitory D2 receptors suppress the indirect movement pathway.

open.q: Compare the G-protein coupling and cAMP effects of D1-like versus D2-like dopamine receptors.
accept: D1-like couple to Gs and increase cAMP; D2-like couple to Gi/o and decrease cAMP
D1 stimulates adenylyl cyclase (Gs); D2 inhibits adenylyl cyclase (Gi)

questions.q: How does a metabotropic (G-protein-coupled) neurotransmitter receptor differ functionally from an ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channel) receptor?
options: Ionotropic receptors act through gene transcription; metabotropic receptors form fast ion channels
Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated channels; metabotropic receptors signal through G proteins and second messengers
Metabotropic receptors never influence membrane ion channels
Ionotropic receptors are found only in the adrenal cortex
questions.explain: Ionotropic receptors (nAChR, AMPA, NMDA, GABA-A, glycine, 5-HT3) mediate rapid synaptic transmission, whereas metabotropic receptors (mAChR, adrenergic, D1/D2, GABA-B, mGluR, neuropeptide GPCRs) mediate slower neuromodulation.

open.q: Contrast ionotropic and metabotropic receptors in terms of structure, response latency, and physiological role.
accept: Ionotropic receptors contain an intrinsic ion channel pore for fast millisecond signaling; metabotropic receptors signal via G-proteins and second messengers for slower, prolonged neuromodulation
Direct ligand-gated ion channels (fast) vs G-protein-coupled second-messenger receptors (slow/modulatory)

questions.q: What is long-term depression (LTD) in cerebellar Purkinje neurons or hippocampal CA1 synapses?
options: A persistent activity-dependent reduction in synaptic strength mediated by phosphatase activation (calcineurin/PP1) and clathrin-dependent endocytosis (internalization) of postsynaptic AMPA receptors
A permanent doubling of postsynaptic AMPA receptors
Overgrowth of myelin across the synaptic cleft
Conversion of inhibitory synapses into gap junctions
questions.explain: Moderate, prolonged Ca2+ elevation (or coincident parallel-fiber + climbing-fiber activation in the cerebellum) activates protein phosphatases that dephosphorylate AMPA receptors and trigger their endocytosis, refining motor learning and memory.

open.q: Describe the postsynaptic receptor trafficking mechanism responsible for long-term depression (LTD).
accept: Protein phosphatase activation triggers dephosphorylation and endocytosis (internalization) of postsynaptic AMPA receptors, reducing synaptic responsiveness
Internalization/removal of AMPA receptors from the postsynaptic membrane

questions.q: Which serotonin receptor subtype is the ONLY ionotropic (ligand-gated cation channel) serotonin receptor, clinically targeted by antiemetic drugs such as ondansetron?
options: 5-HT1A receptor
5-HT2A receptor
5-HT3 receptor
5-HT4 receptor
questions.explain: All serotonin receptors (5-HT1 through 5-HT7) are G-protein-coupled receptors EXCEPT 5-HT3, which is a pentameric ligand-gated cation channel in the area postrema and vagal afferents blocked by ondansetron to prevent chemotherapy-induced vomiting.

open.q: Identify the sole ionotropic serotonin receptor subtype and name a selective antagonist used clinically as an antiemetic.
accept: 5-HT3 receptor; ondansetron (or granisetron)
5-HT3; ondansetron

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with fluctuating diplopia, bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, and proximal limb weakness that worsens toward the evening and improves with rest. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental compound muscle action potential response, and intravenous edrophonium rapidly restores muscle strength. Which autoantibody causes myasthenia gravis?
options: Autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
IgG autoantibodies directed against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (Nm) at the neuromuscular junction, causing complement-mediated receptor destruction and internalization
Autoantibodies against spinal glycine receptors
Autoantibodies against oligodendrocyte myelin basic protein
questions.explain: Loss of functional postsynaptic Nm receptors reduces end-plate potential amplitude below firing threshold during repetitive firing (exhausting the NMJ safety factor); AChE inhibitors (pyridostigmine) raise cleft ACh to compensate.

open.q: Explain how autoantibodies in myasthenia gravis reduce the safety factor of neuromuscular transmission and why acetylcholinesterase inhibitors improve strength.
accept: Autoantibodies destroy/internalize postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors, lowering EPP amplitude below threshold during repeated activity; AChE inhibitors prolong ACh in the cleft so remaining receptors are activated
Reduced postsynaptic Nm receptor density lowers EPP; AChE inhibition increases synaptic ACh concentration

questions.q: A 61-year-old chronic smoker presents with proximal lower-limb weakness, dry mouth, and hyporeflexia that paradoxically IMPROVES transiently after brief vigorous muscle contraction, accompanied by an incremental response on high-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation. Chest CT shows a small-cell lung carcinoma. What is the mechanism of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)?
options: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels on motor and autonomic nerve terminals, reducing quantal ACh exocytosis (which builds up Ca2+ during high-frequency activity)
Deficiency of acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft
Autoantibodies against skeletal muscle titin
questions.explain: Unlike myasthenia gravis (postsynaptic Nm attack, worsens with use), LEMS attacks presynaptic P/Q-type Ca2+ channels; repetitive firing accumulates residual presynaptic Ca2+ to boost ACh release and temporarily improve strength.

open.q: Contrast the target antigen and the effect of repetitive muscle contraction in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) versus myasthenia gravis.
accept: LEMS targets presynaptic P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and strength improves with brief exercise (Ca2+ accumulation); myasthenia gravis targets postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors and weakness worsens with use
Presynaptic Ca2+ channel autoantibodies with post-exercise facilitation (LEMS) vs postsynaptic Nm autoantibodies with fatigability (MG)

questions.q: A 40-year-old agricultural worker is brought to the emergency department after accidental exposure to an organophosphate insecticide (parathion), exhibiting pinpoint pupils (miosis), profuse salivation, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, diarrhea, and skeletal muscle fasciculations followed by paralysis. How do atropine and pralidoxime (2-PAM) treat this poisoning?
options: Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic ACh receptors (reversing SLUDGE/bronchorrhea/bradycardia), while pralidoxime regenerates phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase before 'aging' occurs (restoring nicotinic NMJ function)
Atropine activates nicotinic receptors; pralidoxime destroys acetylcholine
Both drugs block voltage-gated Na+ channels
Atropine blocks GABA-A receptors; pralidoxime stimulates renin
questions.explain: Organophosphates irreversibly phosphorylate the serine hydroxyl group of AChE; atropine blocks central and peripheral muscarinic excess (including life-threatening bronchorrhea) but does not act at nicotinic NMJs, whereas 2-PAM cleaves the phosphate-enzyme bond to reactivate AChE.

open.q: Explain why both atropine and pralidoxime (2-PAM) are required in the management of severe organophosphate poisoning.
accept: Atropine blocks excessive muscarinic receptor stimulation (bronchorrhea, bradycardia), whereas pralidoxime reactivates inhibited acetylcholinesterase to relieve nicotinic depolarizing neuromuscular paralysis
Atropine antagonizes muscarinic symptoms; pralidoxime regenerates AChE to reverse nicotinic muscle paralysis

questions.q: A 67-year-old man develops resting 'pill-rolling' tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability due to degeneration of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Why is oral L-DOPA combined with carbidopa rather than administering dopamine directly?
options: Dopamine crosses the blood-brain barrier, but L-DOPA does not
L-DOPA crosses the blood-brain barrier; carbidopa limits its peripheral conversion to dopamine
Carbidopa converts dopamine into serotonin inside the liver
Dopamine destroys GABA-A receptors in the striatum
questions.explain: Peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase converts >95% of unprotected L-DOPA into dopamine outside the brain; carbidopa blocks peripheral decarboxylation so more L-DOPA enters the striatum.

open.q: Explain the pharmacological rationale for co-administering carbidopa with L-DOPA in Parkinson's disease.
accept: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase without crossing the blood-brain barrier, preventing peripheral dopamine side effects and increasing the fraction of L-DOPA reaching the brain
Blocks peripheral conversion of L-DOPA to dopamine outside the BBB, increasing central L-DOPA availability

questions.q: A 24-year-old man ingests rodenticide powder in a suicide attempt and develops severe painful extensor muscle spasms, opisthotonus, risus sardonicus, and hyperreflexia while remaining fully awake and alert. Which synaptic receptor is blocked by strychnine poisoning?
options: Postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Postsynaptic inhibitory glycine receptors in the spinal cord and brainstem
Presynaptic opioid mu receptors
Hippocampal NMDA glutamate receptors
questions.explain: Strychnine is a potent competitive antagonist of strychnine-sensitive glycine Cl- channels on spinal motor neurons, abolishing Renshaw and reciprocal inhibition so minimal sensory stimuli trigger violent generalized extensor spasms.

open.q: Identify the neurotransmitter receptor antagonized by strychnine and explain why poisoning produces generalized muscle spasms in an awake patient.
accept: Inhibitory glycine receptors in the spinal cord and brainstem; loss of glycinergic postsynaptic inhibition disinhibits alpha motor neurons
Glycine-gated Cl- channels; blocks spinal inhibitory circuits
